title: Ang 600–608: the third and fourth Gurus
tomorrow: if we all have one Father, who exactly counts as family?

lines: SORRY, BUT HERE'S WHY I WAS RIGHT.
cards: Some apologies come with a speech attached: sorry, but here's why I was right. The sorry gets one word and the defense gets a paragraph. That's the pride still talking, and it's yesterday's question.
The hymns of Guru Amar Das and Guru Ram Das in Sorath, from ang 600, keep coming back to one way the pride goes quiet. They call it the Word.

teach.b: First, how to find your way on these pages. The Gurus all sign their hymns Nanak, so the heading tells you who's speaking: Mahala 3 is Guru Amar Das, Mahala 4 is Guru Ram Das. Here they come in that order.
And their theme in Sorath is the shabad, the Word: the Guru's teaching, heard and taken in. In paraphrase, Guru Amar Das sings that through the Word, haumai, the ego, the I-I-I, is burned away.

teach.h: DYING IN THE WORD: THE EGO GOES QUIET.
teach.b: He speaks of dying in the Word: the proud self going quiet while you're still alive, so that, as he puts it, there's no need to die again.
Without the Word, the self-willed mind keeps wandering in doubt.
Guru Ram Das sings of the same Word as sweet, something you taste rather than argue about. The Word works here the way the seed did yesterday: it goes in quietly, and it changes the ground.
So what do these pages give you this week, for the apology that keeps turning into a speech? Not a technique. A way to let the speech die.
When the Word is louder than the I, the sorry doesn't need a defense. It can just be sorry.

how: In the Guru Granth Sahib each raga's hymns are grouped by Guru, marked Mahala 1, 3, 4, 5 and so on; Sikhs read the Sorath hymns of Guru Amar Das and Guru Ram Das in that order.

games.q: the Word in Sorath — tap the pairs.

s: 'dying in the Word' is about physical death
it's the proud self going quiet while you're alive, so there's no need to die again.
the heading Mahala 3 marks a hymn of Guru Amar Das
the Gurus all sign as Nanak, so the heading says who is speaking.
these Sorath hymns say the Word is something to argue about
Guru Ram Das sings of it as sweet, something tasted.

games.q: you told your sister she was being selfish. she was, a little. you want to make it right. what fits the Word in Sorath?
o: say sorry plainly and leave the 'but' out.
say sorry, then explain why you were partly right.
wait for her to admit her part first, so it's even.
games.why: Guru Amar Das sings of the ego burned away through the Word. the sorry without the speech is what that looks like on an ordinary day.

practice: Bring to mind one sorry you owe, big or small. Picture saying it, and notice the exact moment the 'but' wants to come in; then picture it again, stopping right before that word.
For the rest of the sit, plan one plain sentence you could say, with nothing after it.
